title: ENH: allow setting parameters for BFGS optimizer
body:
This MR adds the parameter `alpha = 1 / H0` known from `LBFGS` to `BFGS` and adds the attribute `BFGS.H0`. This enables to deviate from the initial value of `alpha = 1/70 eV/AA`,

```python
opt = BFGS(..., alpha=25)
```

and further enables to inject custom hessians via

```python
opt.H0 = custom_H0
```

after initialization.
author: flokno

comments.author: askhl
comments.body:
Scaling down the steps and getting negative eigenvalues is quite common, so IMHO not something to *warn* about (although a detailed log should definitely include that information).  In a large system with long-range changes -- imagine a long carbon chain which rotates -- we would consistently get large displacements.

The current maxstep=0.04 is a very bad choice.  A much more reasonable default is 0.2 like the other optimizers.  But changing things is hell, because people's simulations will then run differently.

I think we should write an entirely new optimizer *wrapper* which does all the common stuff: It has reasonable defaults, a single implementation of standard stuff like `replay_trajectory()`, and takes care of things like whether we are writing to a trajectory.  It also does all of the logging which doesn't apply to a particular algorithm.  Those things that *do* apply to a particular algorithm, well, hmm, it could ask the algorithm to print that stuff into a particular file object maybe.

Of course we couldn't do all that by tomorrow...
comments.label_reasoning: The comment primarily critiques the overall design and architecture of the optimizer infrastructure — bad defaults, duplicated common logic across optimizers, and a proposal to refactor into a proper wrapper — which maps best to Structural Issues (code organization and module boundaries).

review_threads.actionability_reasoning: Suggests changing the default maxstep value and proposes writing a new optimizer wrapper with better architecture — concrete improvement suggestions.

comments.author: askhl
comments.body:
As a software library, it's bad style to print to stdout because that stream belongs to the caller.  We can only print to it if the caller explicitly tells us to.

To a lesser extent the same applies to stderr.

Since this can happen for valid geometries, and since the algorithm should recover, it's not truly a job for warnings.warn() either.

We should perhaps start using the `logging` module, but I propose discussing centralized logging in a separate issue.
comments.label_reasoning: The comment flags printing directly to stdout/stderr as bad practice in a library context and recommends using Python's `logging` module instead — a well-known Python-specific convention and idiom.
